\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The choice of which structures to prune from a reasoning LLM determines whether the model can sustain reinforcement learning alignment.
Current compression pipelines treat this choice as independent of downstream training: structured pruning removes entire attention heads or MLP channels to reduce memory and latency~\citep{llmpruner2023,graspprune2026}, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) recovers task accuracy, and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) restores reasoning quality~\citep{deepseek2025r1,shao2024grpo}.
Each stage is optimized in isolation.
We show that this separation fails: the pruning criterion fundamentally controls what we term \textbf{recovery capacity}, the model's ability to sustain RL-based recovery without collapsing into degenerate outputs.

Two findings expose this failure.
First, GRPO reward gains on GSM8K~\citep{cobbe2021gsm8k} do not reflect genuine reasoning improvement.
On an unpruned DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B~\citep{deepseek2025r1}, 100 steps of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO;~\citealp{shao2024grpo}) raise the mean reward from 0 to 0.661, yet greedy accuracy remains exactly 81.27\%, with 1{,}072 of 1{,}319 test problems producing identical correct answers before and after alignment.
The same pattern holds for pruned models: Standard-pruned accuracy is 58.91\% after GRPO versus 59.29\% after SFT ($\Delta{=}{-}0.38$ pp).
Under GSM8K's binary reward with greedy evaluation, reward optimization reshapes output format and sampling properties without solving new problems.
Second, GRPO training on pruned models can trigger complete collapse: gradient norms approach zero, the model produces repetitive outputs, and reward degrades monotonically.
\citet{selfhealing2025} claim that RLVR recovers pruned reasoning models to 95\%+ of original performance, but their evaluation uses a single pruning method and reports only final-checkpoint accuracy without examining training dynamics.

Existing structured pruning methods for reasoning LLMs optimize for post-pruning quality without studying downstream alignment.
GRASPrune~\citep{graspprune2026} introduces global gating for budgeted compression.
RESP~\citep{resp2025} uses reasoning-trace calibration.
LLM-Pruner~\citep{llmpruner2023} and Bonsai~\citep{bonsai2025} target general LLM compression.
PASER~\citep{paser2025} optimizes recovery data selection, and PAT~\citep{pat2025} proposes pruning-aware tuning.
None compare multiple pruning criteria under RL alignment or study how pruning affects RL training dynamics.
\citet{rlsqueezes2026} show that RL and SFT impose fundamentally different demands on model representations: RL compresses solution paths while SFT expands them.
This divergence suggests that pruning decisions should substantially affect RL trainability, yet no prior work has tested this hypothesis.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{../figures/paper/fig1_framework.pdf}
\caption{Controlled comparison framework. All four pruning criteria share the same structural analysis (Taylor importance + CKA overlap) and identical recovery pipeline (SFT warmup $\to$ GRPO). Despite identical training, the criteria produce divergent outcomes: CKA-only achieves active learning while Standard and \rasp{} collapse.}
\label{fig:framework}
\end{figure}

We present the first controlled comparison of four structural pruning criteria under identical GRPO training on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B at 20\% structured sparsity (Figure~\ref{fig:framework}).
The four criteria span a spectrum of representational diversity preservation: \textbf{CKA-only} scoring removes structures with the highest pairwise Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA;~\citealp{kornblith2019cka}) overlap, preserving all representationally unique structures; \textbf{Random} scoring provides an unbiased baseline; \textbf{Standard} importance-only scoring retains structures with the highest gradient-based importance~\citep{llmpruner2023}; and \textbf{Recovery-Aware Structured Pruning} (\rasp{}) combines importance with CKA overlap in a composite score.
Under identical GRPO configuration, these four methods reveal a \textbf{recovery capacity gradient}.
CKA-only pruning achieves \emph{active learning}: peak reward reaches 0.354 (4.4$\times$ Standard), and the model self-recovers from a transient step-90 dip (0.242$\to$0.344 at step 100).
Random pruning stagnates (reward oscillates 0.14--0.19).
Standard pruning exhibits borderline collapse (peak 0.081, gradient norm drops to 0.017).
\rasp{} collapses permanently (peak 0.061, 85\% of completions yield zero reward variance).

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\subsection{Structured Pruning of Large Language Models}
\label{sec:rw_pruning}

Structured pruning removes entire architectural units (attention heads, MLP channels, or layers) to reduce model size while maintaining hardware-friendly dense computation.
LLM-Pruner~\citep{llmpruner2023} introduced dependency-aware structural pruning that respects inter-component coupling in transformer architectures.
Bonsai~\citep{bonsai2025} achieves competitive structured pruning using only forward passes, eliminating the need for gradient computation.
GRASPrune~\citep{graspprune2026} advances the state of the art with global gating that jointly prunes FFN channels and KV head groups under a unified budget constraint.
ShortGPT~\citep{shortgpt2024} and SliceGPT~\citep{slicegpt2024} target layer-level depth pruning, while Wanda~\citep{wanda2024} addresses unstructured weight sparsity; both are complementary but orthogonal to the width-level structural pruning we study.

For reasoning models specifically, RESP~\citep{resp2025} introduces self-reflective pruning using gradient-based importance on self-generated reasoning traces, achieving 81.3\% on GSM8K at 40\% structured sparsity without recovery training.
SSGR~\citep{ssgr2025} shows that selective self-generated calibration with challenging, moderately-lengthy reasoning examples further improves pruning quality.
\citet{llms2lrms2026} systematically compare width and depth pruning for reasoning-centric models, finding width pruning more robust to reasoning degradation but not studying RLVR recovery.
\citet{doingmore2026} reveal that unstructured pruning can improve test-time scaling for reasoning while structured pruning degrades it, suggesting that \emph{which} structures are removed critically shapes downstream capability.

A parallel line of work recognizes that \emph{functional structure} within networks should guide pruning decisions.
FANG~\citep{fang_2025} groups FFN neurons by functional roles via activation clustering and retains shared neurons to prevent cross-task accuracy loss.
FuncNet~\citep{funcnet_2025} applies Independent Component Analysis to decompose LLMs into functional networks and preserves key neurons within each.
MPruner~\citep{mpruner2024} uses \emph{inter-layer} CKA~\citep{kornblith2019cka} to cluster globally redundant layers for depth pruning in CNNs.
\citet{lachance2024cka} similarly apply CKA-based layer similarity for depth pruning.
These approaches operate at the layer level to identify removable layers.
Our work uses \emph{intra-layer} CKA between individual structures (GQA groups, MLP channels) to measure per-structure functional redundancy, a finer granularity optimizing for a different objective: predicting which pruning criterion enables RL-based recovery rather than preserving immediate accuracy.
Among representation similarity measures, \citet{klabunde_similarity_survey_2025} show that CKA achieves 99.3\% layer identification accuracy versus 45.4\% for SVCCA, supporting its use for comparing heterogeneous structures within the same layer.

None of the above methods compare multiple pruning criteria under RL alignment or study how the pruning decision affects downstream RL training dynamics.

\subsection{Pruning-Aware Recovery}
\label{sec:rw_recovery}

Post-pruning recovery is essential at moderate to high compression ratios.
\citet{selfhealing2025} demonstrate that RLVR recovery restores pruned reasoning models to 95\%+ accuracy at 25\% compression, significantly outperforming SFT recovery (${\sim}$80\%).
This establishes RLVR as the preferred recovery paradigm for reasoning models, but Self-Healing treats the pruning method as a black box and tests only one compression ratio.
It does not study whether the \emph{choice} of what to prune affects how well RLVR can recover, the central question of our work.

$P^2$ Law~\citep{p2law2025} establishes scaling laws for post-training loss after pruning, predicting recovery data requirements at a given compression ratio, but studies only continual pre-training rather than RLVR or SFT.
PASER~\citep{paser2025} optimizes which recovery \emph{data} to use through manifold learning and capability-aware budget allocation.
PAT~\citep{pat2025} shows that jointly considering pruning and fine-tuning objectives outperforms the sequential prune-then-finetune pipeline.
RestoreLCC~\citep{restorelcc_2025} proposes a plug-and-play recovery method that contrastively probes critical attention heads and injects lost activation components back into the pruned model.
\citet{boiling_frog_2026} adopt an iterative prune-tune loop that gradually compresses reasoning models, avoiding abrupt performance collapse through incremental SFT recovery.
These approaches optimize complementary axes: PASER optimizes recovery \emph{data}, PAT optimizes \emph{joint training}, RestoreLCC optimizes post-hoc \emph{compensation}, and Boiling Frog optimizes the \emph{schedule} of pruning-recovery iterations.
Our work isolates a different factor: which \emph{pruning criterion} enables RL-based recovery.

The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis~\citep{frankle2019lth} asks which subnetworks can train effectively from random initialization.
Our recovery capacity gradient extends this notion to what we term \emph{paradigm-conditioned trainability}: the optimal subnetwork depends not only on the task but on the recovery paradigm (RLVR vs.\ SFT), as each paradigm imposes fundamentally different functional requirements on the retained architecture.

\subsection{RLVR Training Dynamics}
\label{sec:rw_rlvr}

Understanding how RLVR reshapes model representations is central to predicting which pruned structures support recovery.
\citet{rlsqueezes2026} show that RLVR and SFT shape reasoning capabilities through fundamentally different mechanisms: RLVR \emph{compresses} incorrect reasoning trajectories via global exploration, while SFT \emph{expands} correct trajectories via local imitation.
This asymmetry is the conceptual foundation for our finding that gradient importance scoring harms RL recovery: structures that RL would compress anyway are precisely those that gradient importance protects.
OPSD~\citep{opsd2026} proposes a post-RL compaction stage that further compresses reasoning traces after RLVR training, reinforcing the view that RLVR-trained models exhibit compressible internal structure.

RL training instability in language models has been studied primarily in the RLHF context.
\citet{gao2023overoptimization} characterize reward overoptimization as a systematic failure mode where reward model scores increase while true quality degrades.
\citet{dong2025rlplus} document RL+ collapse where policy models degenerate into repetitive outputs during extended RL training, producing high-reward but low-quality text.
\citet{shah2025comedy} analyze the interaction between reward estimation and policy optimization, showing that biased reward signals compound during training.
Our work connects this instability literature to structural pruning: we show that the pruning criterion determines whether a model is susceptible to RL collapse, with gradient importance scoring pushing models into the collapse regime while CKA-based scoring provides resilience.

\begin{abstract}
Structured pruning of reasoning Large Language Models (LLMs) is typically followed by Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to recover reasoning ability.
The standard pipeline treats the pruning decision as independent of the downstream RL alignment stage.
We show that this independence assumption is wrong: the pruning criterion determines whether the model can sustain RL training at all.
Through a controlled comparison of four structural pruning criteria on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B at 20\% sparsity under identical Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) training, we discover a \emph{recovery capacity gradient}.
CKA-only pruning, which removes only functionally redundant structures measured by Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), achieves active learning with peak reward 0.354 and self-recovery from mid-training perturbations.
Random pruning stagnates (peak 0.190).
Standard importance-only pruning exhibits borderline collapse (peak 0.081, gradient norm drops to 0.017).
Recovery-Aware Structured Pruning (RASP) collapses permanently (peak 0.061).
The gradient follows preserved representational diversity: gradient importance scoring, the industry standard, removes structures that are representationally unique, destroying the exploration capacity that RL requires.
Separately, we observe that GRPO reward-accuracy decoupling on GSM8K is an in-distribution saturation effect: reward rises from 0 to 0.661 for the unpruned model while accuracy remains unchanged at 81.27\%.
Our results establish that pruning criterion selection is the dominant factor in post-pruning RL trainability, and that CKA-based scoring is a simple, effective alternative to gradient importance for RL-intended compression.
\end{abstract}

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We present the first controlled multi-method comparison showing that structural pruning criterion determines post-RLVR recovery capacity of reasoning LLMs.
Under identical GRPO training, four pruning criteria at 20\% sparsity produce qualitatively distinct outcomes: CKA-only pruning enables active learning with self-recovery (peak reward 0.354, 4.4$\times$ Standard), Random pruning stagnates, and gradient importance-based methods (Standard, RASP) collapse.
This recovery capacity gradient reveals that gradient importance scoring, the industry standard for structured pruning, is actively harmful for post-pruning RL alignment because it removes representationally unique structures that RL exploration requires.

CKA-only scoring provides an actionable alternative: it preserves all functionally unique structures by removing only those with high pairwise CKA overlap, requires no gradient computation, and produces both the best RL recovery and the best SFT recovery (63.91\% vs 59.29\% for Standard, $p{\approx}0.015$).
A universal sparsity cliff at 30\% bounds the operating regime for this finding: the recovery capacity gradient is meaningful at 20--25\% sparsity.

Our work has several limitations.
We evaluate on a single base model (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) and a single reasoning benchmark (GSM8K).
GRPO training is limited to 100 steps; extended training may change the dynamics.
The sparsity cliff at 30\% constrains applicability to moderate compression ratios.

Future work should validate the recovery capacity gradient across model families and scales, explore whether adaptive CKA thresholds can push the sparsity cliff beyond 30\%, and investigate the interaction between pruning criterion and other RL algorithms beyond GRPO.
